newsitem.title: USA: Wealthy women more likely to pass on money to kids.
newsitem.headline: Wealthy women more likely to pass on money to kids.

text.p: Wealthy men and women agree on the need to be financially secure, but wealthy women are more likely to emphasise providing for their children's educations or leaving them an inheritance, a study said Wednesday.

According to the study of about 200 of the wealthiest Americans, men and women differed markedly in their approach to issues such as their children's financial security, risk-taking and the use of financial advisers.

Wealty women indicated in the survey a stronger focus on their children's financal security. When asked about reasons to value money, three-quarters of the women, but only half of the men, said "it enables you to give advantages to your children."

More than half of the women, 53 percent, stated the importance of providing for their children's education, compared with 40 percent of the men. Leaving an inheritance to family members was a goal for almost half of the women, but only a third of the men.

Women rated several goals for their children more highly then men, including earning enough to support a family (95 percent of women, 81 percent of men); being able to enjoy life's luxuries (66 percent vs. 44 percent); never having to worry about money (59 percent vs. 36 percent); doing better financially than their parents (57 percent vs. 36 percent) and supporting charities (51 percent vs. 36 percent).
In estate planning, affluent women were more likely than men to change their lifestyle so to leave their children a larger inheritance.
"I think the difference in men and women's attitudes toward children reflects varying approaches to the same end," said Jeffrey S. Maurer, president of U.S. Trust, which sponsored the study.

"Both are concerned about their children, but women are more interested in providing a financial cushion for their offspring, while men feel it is better for the children if they have to work a little harder to be succesful on their own."

The survey also showed that women are more averse to risk than men. Fifty-four percent of the women preferred safer investments, compared with 45 percent of the men. Only 20 percent of women preferred riskier investments, compared with 37 percent of the men.
Women are also much more likely to consult a professional for financial advice. Seventy-five percent of the women said they use an advisor vs. 54 percent of the men.
Meanwhile about two thirds of women said their husbands were their most important source of financial advise, while only 26 percent of the men said the same for their wives.

"Just as they are reluctant to ask for directions when they are lost, men seem to be more reticent about seeking financial advice. They're more likely to try to handle their finances themselves," Maurer said.

The survey of 202 individuals, each with an adjusted gross income of more than $200,000 annually or a net worth greater than $3 million, was prepared by Financial Market Research Inc. of New York for U.S. Trust.
